Question: What will happen if we don’t declare the main as static?
Answer: Java 22 has some syntax sugar where the above is a full Java program. It does hide some deep magic though. Previously, your main() function had to be static. That marks the method as not being an object instance method, but being a very different beast called a class instance method. Object methods implicitly know about the insides of a single object. An object is an instance, created by the new keyword, of a Class. A class instance method knows about the class itself. With the older system, if you removed the static from main() it just would not compile. Java needs a class-method called main() (which in turn needs to be marked as static) or else it cannot start up.

Question: In Java, is it possible to create primitive types that are stand-alone (that is, primitives that are not object members or array elements) directly on the heap as you can in C++ (e.g. int* i= new int)? If so, how?
Answer: Sort of. Makes an object on the heap that holds exactly one integer. It’s not just an integer; it has all the other things required in an instance of class Object. I don’t think we can do this any more directly; but it’s not something I have ever concerned myself with. Practically, the heap is used to hold object instances. Primitives can be parts of those object instances, where they make sense. Maybe the object only needs one primitive, given its intended purpose. It’s worth noting that Java is not C++ and so a lot of C++ specific thinking simply does not apply.
